h1: The 8 Best Thermal Scopes of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 8 thermal scopes for lawful hunting and pest control, scored on sensor resolution, refresh rate, range and battery life.
summary: The AGM Rattler V2 35-384 is the thermal scope to buy if you want a 384x288 sensor, a stated 1,800 yard detection range and 11 hours of battery in one durable body. The oneleaf.ai Mars MT1000LRF is the sharpest image here, with a 640x512 sensor, 60Hz refresh and a built-in rangefinder, and the GOYOJO GRL325 is the best step-up value under $1,000. The AGM 256-sensor models and the RIX Storm S2 are the entry route for pest control and shorter shots.
intro: The usual thermal scope mistake is shopping for the biggest detection-range number on the box. Detection range only tells you that a warm shape is visible as a blob. Whether you can tell a hog from a deer, or a coyote from a stray dog, depends on sensor resolution and lens size, and that is where a 640x512 sensor and a 256x192 sensor feel like different products.

This ranking covers eight thermal imaging scopes used for lawful hunting and pest control, from the $500 to $1,000 bracket up to premium units over $1,000. We reviewed the listed sensor resolution, lens, refresh rate, detection range, battery life and weather rating, and we rank them on how clearly they let you identify a target. Always follow local hunting laws and positively identify your target and what is behind it.

products.name: AGM Global Vision Rattler V2 35-384 Thermal Scope
products.verdict: A balanced 384x288 scope with a 35mm lens, 1,800 yard detection and 11 hours of battery.
products.description:
The Rattler V2 35-384 pairs a 384x288 12 micron thermal sensor with a 35mm germanium lens and an OLED display. AGM lists a detection range of up to 1,800 yards, 3x base magnification with up to 24x digital zoom, and about 11 hours of continuous operation on a rechargeable battery. It carries an IP67 rating, shot-activated recording and a Wi-Fi hotspot.

It ranks first because it is the best all-rounder on paper. The oneleaf.ai Mars units below have the higher-resolution 640x512 sensor and 60Hz refresh, but they cost more in complexity and lean on interchangeable lenses sold separately. The AGM keeps one lens, a stated battery life and a waterproof body, which is what most users actually want.

It is the pick for hunters who want a dependable scope for field work without chasing every spec. The caveat is that digital zoom beyond the base 3x softens the image, so treat the 24x figure as a convenience and not a substitute for resolution.
products.idealFor: Hunters who want one dependable scope for hogs, coyotes and predator control.
products.skipIf: You want the highest sensor resolution and rangefinder.

products.name: oneleaf.ai Mars MT1000LRF 35mm Thermal Scope
products.verdict: A 640x512 sensor, 60Hz refresh, a rangefinder and a ballistic calculator in one unit.
products.description:
The Mars MT1000LRF in this version ships with a 35mm lens at 2x base magnification and a 640x512 12 micron sensor with sensitivity below 20mK. The listing states detection out to 1,969 yards, a refresh rate selectable at 30, 50 or 60Hz, and 1x to 8x digital zoom. A built-in rangefinder reaches up to 1,300 yards, and the ballistic calculator stores seven sets of data.

It lands second because the sensor is the best resolution in the guide, and the 60Hz refresh rate smooths motion on moving animals. The AGM above has a simpler package and a stated battery life, which the listing here does not clearly match. A 35mm lens at 2x also gives a wide view for scanning rather than long identification.

Buy it if image quality and onboard tools matter most. The caveat is that the 50mm lens is sold separately, and the price sits over $1,000.
products.idealFor: Experienced users who want maximum detail and onboard distance tools.
products.skipIf: You want a simple scope with fewer menus.

products.name: oneleaf.ai 640x512 Thermal Scope with 50mm Lens
products.verdict: The same 640x512 platform with a 50mm F1.0 lens at 2.8x for longer identification.
products.description:
This version uses a 640x512 12 micron sensor with sensitivity below 20mK behind a 50mm F1.0 lens at 2.8x base magnification, reaching up to 22x maximum. It focuses from 3.28 yards to infinity, offers 70mm eye relief with a -6 to +2 diopter range, six reticle types and 5 colors, plus a rangefinder, a ballistic calculator and 30, 50 or 60Hz refresh.

It ranks third because the 35mm Mars gives a wider scanning view for similar money, while this 50mm unit narrows the field for longer identification. The F1.0 aperture gathers more heat energy for a cleaner image, which is the real benefit. The AGM 35-384 at the top is the lighter-decision choice, with less setup.

Choose it if your shots are longer and you want the extra reach of a bigger lens. The caveat is that the 35mm and 75mm lenses are extra purchases, and a bigger objective adds weight and cost.
products.idealFor: Users who want longer-range identification on the same 640x512 platform.
products.skipIf: You scan close brush and prefer a wider view.

products.name: AGM Global Vision Rattler V2 25-384 Thermal Scope
products.verdict: A 384x288 sensor in a 25mm package with 880 yard detection and 50Hz refresh.
products.description:
The Rattler V2 25-384 uses a 384x288 12 micron VOx sensor with a 25mm germanium lens, a 3.5x base magnification and an OLED display. The listing gives 880 yards of detection range, a 50Hz refresh rate and built-in video and still capture to internal storage.

It ranks fourth because the 35mm sibling above detects out to 1,800 yards on the same sensor class, which is the cost of the smaller lens. The GOYOJO below has a similar sensor and a higher stated detection range, but it is also cheaper. Within AGM's line this is the one that suits short and mid-range work.

It makes sense for pest control and yard-length shots. The caveat is that the listing does not state battery life, so confirm the runtime before a long hunt, and the price sits over $1,000.
products.idealFor: Short and mid-range pest control and property work.
products.skipIf: You want longer reach for the same sensor class.

products.name: GOYOJO GRL325 Thermal Riflescope
products.verdict: A 384x288 sensor with a 1024x768 OLED, 55Hz refresh and 64GB of storage for under $1,000.
products.description:
The GRL325 combines a 25mm lens, a 384x288 sensor with sensitivity below 25mK, a 1024x768 OLED display and a stated detection range of 1,546 yards. It offers 3x to 12x magnification, 55Hz refresh, seven imaging modes and recoil-activated video onto 64GB of internal storage, with an app for live streaming. It is rated IP65 and quotes 6 to 8 hours of operation.

It ranks fifth because the 6 to 8 hour runtime and IP65 rating trail the AGM Rattler's 11 hours and IP67. That gap is the price of the bracket. Against the RIX below, it adds a higher sensor resolution, a bigger display and a longer detection claim.

It is the right buy for those who want a 384 sensor under $1,000. The caveat is the shorter battery life, so carry a spare power source, and the water protection suits rain but not full immersion.
products.idealFor: Value-focused hunters stepping up from a 256 sensor.
products.skipIf: You regularly hunt in heavy rain for long sits.

products.name: RIX Storm S2 256x192 Thermal Scope
products.verdict: A 0.9 lb aluminum scope with glove-friendly controls and image enhancement.
products.description:
The Storm S2 is a 256x192 scope with a 25mm lens, 3.5x base magnification and a 7.0 degree horizontal field of view. RIX states detection up to 1,422 yards, magnification up to 14x, a weight of about 0.9 lb, aluminum construction, 32GB of onboard storage and Wi-Fi with an app. It adds five image modes and RET image enhancement.

It ranks sixth because a 256x192 sensor identifies less detail than the 384 and 640 models ahead of it, whatever the range figure says. RET processing sharpens the picture, but it cannot add data the sensor never captured. The weight is a real advantage, since a lighter scope eases handheld scanning and mounting.

Choose it for lightweight setups and pest control at moderate distances. The caveat is that the listing does not state battery life, so confirm that before relying on it for long nights.
products.idealFor: Users who want a light, handheld-friendly scope for pest control.
products.skipIf: Identification at distance is your priority.

products.name: AGM Global Vision Rattler V2 25-256 Thermal Scope
products.verdict: A 256x192 scope with a 25mm lens, 1,250 yard detection and a long 11.5 hour battery.
products.description:
The Rattler V2 25-256 has a 256x192 12 micron sensor, a 25mm germanium lens at 3.5x base magnification and a stated detection range of 1,250 yards. It runs up to 11.5 hours with a removable power system and includes two rechargeable batteries, plus 10 reticle options, up to 8x digital zoom and a stadiametric rangefinder. It is rated IP67 and operates down to -22 degrees Fahrenheit.

It ranks seventh because the sensor resolution is the entry level in the AGM family, so it identifies less than the 384 models. What it earns is endurance: two removable batteries and 11.5 hours beat most scopes here at any price. It sits below the RIX in the ranking order only because the RIX is lighter and has a bigger lens-to-weight ratio.

It suits long sits where battery life matters. The caveat is that lower resolution makes long-range identification harder, so keep shots close to the range it was built for.
products.idealFor: Long overnight sits where battery life matters most.
products.skipIf: You need detailed identification at long distance.

products.name: AGM Global Vision Rattler V2 19-256 Thermal Scope
products.verdict: A 19mm lens at 2.5x with a wide view for close scanning and fast-moving targets.
products.description:
The Rattler V2 19-256 pairs a 256x192 12 micron sensor with a 19mm lens at 2.5x base magnification, giving the widest field of view in the AGM line. AGM states up to 11.5 hours of runtime with two rechargeable batteries, 10 reticle styles, 4 colors, 8x digital zoom and a stadiametric rangefinder. It has IP67 waterproofing and runs from -22 to 131 degrees Fahrenheit, and it falls in the $500 to $1,000 bracket.

It ranks last because the small lens and the 256 sensor give the shortest reach here, and the listing gives no detection range figure. That is the tradeoff for the wide field: the scope is built for close brush and moving animals, not for far identification.

Buy it for close-range pest control and thick cover. The caveat is that wide fields sacrifice magnification, so anything farther than a short distance will look small and soft.
products.idealFor: Close scanning in thick brush and quick target acquisition.
products.skipIf: You need to identify targets at long distance.

whatMatters.detail: The sensor is the grid of heat-sensitive pixels, and more pixels mean more detail on a distant shape. A 640x512 sensor holds far more information than a 256x192 one. Look for the resolution in the title, since a marketing detection range does not tell you how well you can identify.

Detection range is how far a warm shape shows up at all, not how far you can recognize it. Identification range is always shorter, and it depends on resolution and lens size. Treat a 1,800 yard figure as a ceiling, and always positively identify your target and what is behind it.

Refresh rate in hertz is how many times per second the image updates. A 60Hz display tracks a moving animal smoothly, while a lower rate can stutter. The Mars scopes allow 30, 50 or 60Hz, and the GOYOJO runs at 55Hz.

A larger lens gathers more heat signal and narrows the field of view. A 19mm lens at 2.5x suits close scanning, a 35mm at 3x balances both, and a 50mm at 2.8x reaches farther. Check the base magnification, because digital zoom only enlarges the same pixels.

Thermal scopes drain batteries in cold air, so a stated 11 hours may shrink in winter. Look for IP67 if you hunt in rain, since IP65 resists spray rather than immersion. Removable batteries, as on the AGM 256 models, extend a night in the field.

howToChoose.intro: Resolution is the single biggest driver of identification quality.

faq.q: Do thermal scopes work in daylight?
faq.a: Yes, they read heat rather than light, so they work in daylight and in dark. Some scopes, such as the oneleaf.ai Mars, offer 11 palettes to adapt to bright, hot ground.

faq.q: What is the most common buying mistake?
faq.a: Choosing by detection range alone. The AGM 35-384 states 1,800 yards, but identification range is shorter. Compare sensor resolution and lens size before you compare range numbers.

faq.q: Is a 384 sensor worth it over a 256?
faq.a: For identification at distance, yes. The GOYOJO GRL325 and AGM 25-384 show far more detail than the RIX Storm S2 or AGM 256 models, and the gap grows with range.

faq.q: How long does the battery last in the cold?
faq.a: Listed runtimes are for mild conditions. The AGM 25-256 quotes 11.5 hours and the GOYOJO 6 to 8, but expect less in freezing weather and carry a spare.

faq.q: Do I need to zero a thermal scope?
faq.a: Yes, mounting and zeroing follow the manufacturer manual. The AGM and Mars units include reticles and a ballistic setup, but check your local laws and use a qualified gunsmith if you are unsure.

faq.q: Can I use a thermal scope handheld?
faq.a: Not as a primary viewer. The RIX Storm S2 is light at about 0.9 lb, but a scope is built to be mounted. For scanning on foot, a dedicated handheld thermal monocular is a better tool.

finalTake: Buy the AGM Rattler V2 35-384 if you want one dependable scope with a 384 sensor and 11 hours of battery. Choose the oneleaf.ai Mars MT1000LRF if image quality and a built-in rangefinder matter most, and the GOYOJO GRL325 if you want a 384 sensor under $1,000. Treat 256 sensors as a short-range tool. Always follow local laws and identify your target and what is behind it.
